Question: What is the best way to learn syntax of any programming language?
Answer: Syntax has no meaning when what you’re doing is not real. You might force yourself to memorize it, but as soon as 72 hours or so pass, you’ll have forgotten it all. To make it real, you must see tangible results when you’re writing code. That means, first of all, solving a problem by trying something out, then experimenting and seeing different outcomes until you’re satisfied. In the process of this tinkering, you will acquire muscle memory and also get used to the syntax without forcing yourself to memorize. If you’re a beginner, find interesting puzzles that give you immediate feedback when you try something new. One such is writing a game in Unity (in C#), which is both fun and rewarding. But that’s for advanced beginners. Total beginners should try Apple’s Swift Playgrounds. Contrary to some bloggers, it’s NOT for children, and it’s NOT easy. It starts off easy but by the end of first main book called “Let’s Code 1” (there are three main books), it becomes quite challenging if you’re willing to push yourself! (meaning, yes, theoretically even a child can solve it, but those solutions will be noobish). By this I mean, try to write better solutions: compact, error-proof, and elegant. Question: Why does Python allow usage of the else keyword after for and while loops?
Answer: Python is the only modern language that allows using an else within/after a while loop, but the concept was taken from “Dijkstra’s Guarded Loop” which was defined in The Guarded Command Language (GCL) and later adopted by Oberon-07: So, this partially answers the why, since it shows historical influences. The motivation for this arises for ‘what to do when the while loop terminates?’. Suppose you have a lemonade stand. (I love lemonades, if it wasn’t obvious). So while we have lemonade in stock, keep informing about sales and how many are left. Now, when no more cups are left, the while loop terminates but the else-clause takes over to print a final message. But functionality-wise, the purpose is mostly syntactic sugar, since it’s strictly not needed. Consider the same in C#, achieved without else-clause: Ditto for 99% of all other languages. But what if the loop breaks? Now the else block won’t run because, as you can see, the loop broke midway. The utility of this? Using an else clause with a loop is a clever way to check if the loop completed normally without encountering a break statement. But as I said, in other languages we can do the same, just not in the same way. Ruby: PHP: ———
